Senses.Explanation: The first position in Dongshan Liangjie's Five Ranks, conventionally called “the biased within the upright.” Caoshan Benji supplies the corpus's direct definition. He identifies the upright position with the empty realm, originally without a thing, and the biased position with the realm of forms and its myriad shapes; he then defines this rank as “turning one's back on principle and going to affairs” (正中偏者，背理就事). In his ruler-and-minister relation, the upright is the ruler, the biased is the minister, and the ruler looking at the minister is this rank (君視臣是正中偏). Dongshan Liangjie's verse places its opening image before the moon is bright in the first night-watch and says that people meet without recognizing one another (正中偏，三更初夜月明前。莫怪相逢不相識，隱隱猶懷舊日嫌). Later speakers keep the rank active in public questioning: asked what it is, Hongzhi Zhengjue answers, “After the clouds disperse from the long sky, the moon shines in the empty hall” (如何是正中偏？師曰：雲散長空後，虗堂夜月明). Baizhang Ruibai Mingxue maps the paired ranks onto Linji terms and says that this rank removes the person, while “the upright within the biased” removes the object (正中偏奪人也，偏中正奪境也). The phrase occurs 329 times in 99 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: Dongshan Liangjie owns the rank verse; Caoshan Benji owns the direct definition and ruler-and-minister relation. Those attributions must not be collapsed. Independent lamp collections preserve both, Dongshan's own record preserves his verse, and Caoshan's own record preserves his definition. This rank is paired with and reverses “the upright within the biased”: turning from principle to affairs versus leaving affairs for principle, and ruler looking at minister versus minister facing ruler.
